notes.meaning: God spoke to Zechariah nearly two years after his earlier night visions. The rebuilding of the temple was now well underway and about halfway finished. The message arrived in late autumn, in the month called Chislev.

A group from the town of Bethel was sent to Jerusalem to pray and seek God's favor. Men named Sharezer and Regem-melech led the delegation. They came to the temple site to ask an official question about religious duties.

The messengers asked the priests and prophets whether they should keep fasting and mourning in the fifth month. For seventy years of exile, the Jews had used that month to mourn the burning of Solomon's temple. Now that the new temple was rising, they wondered if that season of sadness was still needed.

The Lord of Hosts gave Zechariah the answer to this question. The prophet did not speak his own ideas, but delivered a message given directly by God. The Lord had words not only for the visitors, but for the entire community.

God told Zechariah to question both the priests and all the people about their motives. Over the past seventy years, they had fasted in the fifth month for the burned temple and in the seventh month for their murdered governor. God asked them plainly if they had truly observed those days for Him, or simply out of self-pity and human tradition.

God pointed out that their feasting and regular meals were also entirely self-centered. When they ate and drank, they did so only for their own pleasure and nourishment, not to honor the Lord. Their ordinary lives were lived for themselves rather than for God's glory.

Zechariah reminded them of the message God sent through the prophets before the exile began. In those earlier days, Jerusalem and the surrounding towns and foothills were crowded, peaceful, and wealthy. If their ancestors had obeyed God's moral commands back then, the city would never have been destroyed, and these sad fasts would never have been needed.

The word of the Lord came again to Zechariah with direct instructions for the people. God told him to repeat the essential rules of life that the older prophets had preached. The Lord wanted them to know that His moral demands had never changed.

The Lord commanded the people to act with genuine justice and fair judgment. He told them to show tender mercy, kindness, and faithful love toward one another. Living right toward other people pleases God far more than any outward ritual or fasting.

God warned them not to take advantage of vulnerable people like widows, orphans, foreigners, and the poor. He also commanded them never to nurse grudges or secretly plot harm against one another in their minds. True godliness protects the weak and keeps the heart clean from malice.

Earlier generations stubbornly refused to listen to these commands. They pulled their shoulders away like a rebellious ox that refuses to wear a plow's wooden harness. They shut their ears so they would not have to hear God's voice.

The people made their hearts as hard as flint, the toughest stone known to them, so they would not absorb God's law. They rejected the messages that the Holy Spirit gave through the earlier prophets. Because of this deliberate hardness, the Lord of Hosts became very angry with them.

God had called out to their ancestors through His prophets, but the people would not pay attention. Later, when war and disaster struck, the people cried out in terror for help. Because they had ignored God during times of ease, God refused to hear their desperate cries.

The Lord scattered them into exile like a sudden, violent windstorm, driving them among foreign nations they did not know. Behind them, the beautiful land of promise was left empty and ruined, with no travelers passing through. It was the people's own persistent sin that turned their lovely home into a lonely wasteland.
